newsitem.title: USA: US says Swiss handled gold from Holocaust victims.
newsitem.headline: US says Swiss handled gold from Holocaust victims.

text.p: A U.S. study criticized Switzerland on Wednesday for banking Nazi gold during and after World War II and gave gruesome evidence that some gold the Nazis sold to the Swiss had been taken from Holocaust victims.

The study also rapped the U.S. government of the time for not pushing the Swiss hard enough once the war ended to account for and return the millions of dollars worth of gold they had acquired in wartime financial deals with the Nazis.

"The Swiss were handling vast sums of looted gold" in trading with the Third Reich, said the report, compiled by Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat and the State Department's chief historian, William Slaney.

The Reichsbank had an account for melted-down loot from death camp victims, such as rings, coins and even gold teeth, and sold some of this along with gold taken from occupied countries to finance the German war machine, the study said.

"At least a small portion of the gold that entered Switzerland and Italy included non-monetary gold from individual civilians in occupied countries and from concentration camp victims or others killed before they even reached the camps," the study said.
But it stopped short of calling for reopening post-war accords in order to seek more reparations from the Swiss, and Eizenstat did not say whether he thought this should be done.
The study said there was no evidence Swiss officials knew they were buying Holocaust victims' gold, but they did know they bought gold taken from treasuries of occupied countries.

The Swiss said they were shocked by the news. "If this is really true, it is grave news of the most shocking nature," said Thomas Borer, the head of the Swiss government's task force on addressing the Swiss role during and after the war.

"The degree of cynicism and cold-bloodedness it would take for the Nazi brutes to re-melt their victims gold and resell it as regular central bank gold is almost beyond the power of comprehension," Borer told reporters in Washington.
Jewish groups said they were pleased with the study, which took seven months to complete.

"I think the report makes it clear that Switzerland and other countries, neutral and others, are now obligated to deal expeditiously and fully with the challenges of moral and material restitution," said Elan Steinberg, executive director of the World Jewish Congress.
Some of the victims' gold wound up in the gold pool of the commission set up by the allies after the war to return the looted metal to its rightful owners, the report said.

It said the remaining amount in the pool today -- about $70 million -- "is small, but if a significant portion of this amount could be given to Holocaust survivors, it would help them live their declining years in dignity."
Eizenstat said he favored an international conference this fall on the flow of Nazi assets after the war and it would be important to have German records available to trace them.
Britain's new Labour government offered on Tuesday to host such a conference, and Switzerland welcomed the idea.

Switzerland paid $58.1 million in gold in 1946 to a commission set up by the victorious Allies. But the report estimated the amount of looted Nazi gold in the Swiss National Bank was between $185 million and $289 million at the time, and an additional $120 million in German-looted gold was in Swiss bank accounts held by other countries.

Asked whether the 1946 accord setting the amount Switzerland paid should be reopened, Eizenstat told reporters, "At this point we neither exclude nor include the possibility of reopening that agreement."
"Let the report stand for itself at this point, let all the countries involved including Switzerland examine it, determine its credibility, and act accordingly," he said.

In 1952, Switzerland also paid $28 million to the Allies for German assets it had liquidated in Switzerland -- excluding gold -- but the report said that was far less than the actual amount of German assets in the country, estimated at the time at between $250 million and $750 million.

Criticizing the weakness of the U.S. post-war efforts, the study said: "There was a demonstrable lack of senior-level support for a tough U.S. negotiating position with the neutrals (neutral countries)," including Switzerland.
Switzerland recently set up a commission to find assets of Holocaust victims that may still be in Switzerland, and created a $200 million fund for Holocaust victims in need.

Nazi Germany confiscated $580 million of central bank gold -- around $5.6 billion in today's values -- but the amount of other assets they seized, including the Holocaust victims' gold, has not been determined, the report said.

The report also criticized other neutral countries. "It is painfully clear that Argentina, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey and other neutral countries were slow to recognize and acknowledge that this was not just another war .. the fact that they pursued vigorous trade with the Third Reich had the clear effect of supporting and prolonging Nazi Germany's capacity to wage war."
